title: The Amman Message
hookLine: in 2004 hundreds of scholars recognized the eight schools and forbade declaring their followers unbelievers

lines: TAKFIR: CALLING A MUSLIM AN UNBELIEVER.
cards: One word can end a conversation for good. In Arabic it's takfir: declaring another Muslim an unbeliever. Said by the wrong person at the wrong time, it doesn't just insult.
It can put a target on someone's back. Now, Amman, the capital of Jordan, and a different kind of sentence.
Scholars from Sunni, Shia and Ibadi schools, people who disagree about hands in prayer, about the moon, about who should lead, put their names to a list of schools and said: these are all Muslims.

teach.b: In 2004, the Amman Message was issued in Jordan, under King Abdullah the Second, as a statement of what Islam is and is not.
Then a question went to senior scholars of different schools, and their answers became three points. The first: the names.
Whoever follows one of the four Sunni schools, Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i or Hanbali, or the Ja'fari, the Zaydi, the Ibadi or the Zahiri school, is a Muslim.

That's eight, and the schools of these last few days are there by name. The second point is the word from the hook. It is not permitted, the Message says, to declare the followers of these schools unbelievers.
Takfir is closed off between them. Hundreds of scholars endorsed those points, by the Message's own record. The third: who may speak.

A fatwa, a formal legal opinion, belongs to people qualified in a school's method, and no one may issue one outside that method. It's a guard against anyone with a microphone deciding who's in and who's out.
Under all three sits a verse the schools share, in Pickthall's words: "hold fast, all of you together, to the cable of Allah, and do not separate." The Message doesn't erase difference.
The schools still pray with different hands and argue in their books. What it says is that the arguing happens inside one family. Eight schools, one ummah, one community of believers.

how: The Amman Message and its three points recognize eight schools of law, the four Sunni schools with the Ja'fari, Zaydi, Ibadi and Zahiri, forbid declaring their followers unbelievers, and limit fatwas to those qualified in a school's method.

games.q: you're one of the scholars in Amman. someone asks: may a follower of one of these eight schools be declared an unbeliever?
games.why: the Message's second point: it is not permitted to declare the followers of these schools unbelievers.

practice: Say the eight names slowly, one per breath: Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i, Hanbali, Ja'fari, Zaydi, Ibadi, Zahiri, and notice which ones you know a little now and which still feel like strangers.
Then hold one person whose practice differs from yours, in any faith or none, with the thought: we disagree, and we're still neighbors. If you pray, you can pray for unity among those who pray.
